questions.question: What does a Go backend interview cover and why does it exist? It assesses your grasp of Go's concurrency model, its standard library, and how you build production services — the skills a Go shop needs before hiring you.
questions.title: Go Backend Interview Overview
questions.direct_answer: A Go backend interview evaluates your understanding of Go's distinctive features — goroutines and channels, the interface system, error handling, the standard library, and building HTTP services — at the level the role demands (fresher to intermediate). It exists because Go is opinionated and different from Java/Python: its concurrency model, its 'no exceptions' error handling, and its interface satisfaction-by-structure shape how you write production code, and an interviewer must verify you've internalized those idioms before hiring you to write them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand what a Go interview uniquely tests — concurrency (goroutines/channels/select), interfaces (implicit satisfaction), error handling (no exceptions, explicit errors), and the stdlib (net/http, context) — not just 'Go syntax'.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating a Go interview as a generic backend interview with different syntax — missing that it tests Go-specific idioms (channels over locks where possible, errors-as-values, implicit interfaces, context propagation).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame the Go interview as testing four Go-specific pillars: concurrency (goroutines/channels/select), the interface system (implicit, structural), error handling (values, not exceptions), and the stdlib (net/http, context) — plus general backend depth (design, DB, production).

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: A Go backend interview evaluates your understanding of Go's distinctive features at the level the role demands. It exists because Go is opinionated and different from Java/Python: its concurrency model (goroutines and channels), its 'no exceptions' error handling, and its interface satisfaction-by-structure shape how production code is written, and an interviewer must verify you've internalized those idioms before hiring you. The interview typically spans language fundamentals, concurrency, the standard library, building HTTP services, testing, and production concerns — plus general backend depth like system design and databases.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The four Go-specific pillars a Go interview tests: (1) concurrency — goroutines (lightweight threads), channels (typed communication), select (multiplexing), and the sync package (mutex, WaitGroup) for shared state; (2) interfaces — Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly (structural typing, no 'implements'), which changes how you design for testability; (3) error handling — errors are values returned, not exceptions thrown; you check them explicitly and wrap them (errors.Is/As, fmt.Errorf with %w); (4) the standard library — net/http for servers, context for cancellation/timeouts, encoding/json, io for streaming. Plus general backend depth: system design, databases (database/sql), testing (table-driven tests), and production (observability, graceful shutdown).

sections.title: What a Go Interview Tests vs a Generic Backend Interview
A goroutine, a channel, and an error return — the Go idioms
Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension is Go's simplicity versus the patterns you may miss from other languages: Go deliberately omits features (generics were added late, no exceptions, no inheritance) in favor of a small, composable language — the interview tests whether you work with that grain (channels, interfaces, errors-as-values) rather than fighting it. A second tension: concurrency is Go's strength but also its sharpest edge — goroutines are cheap but leak easily, and the interview probes whether you manage cancellation (context) and lifecycle (WaitGroups, channel close) correctly. The third: implicit interfaces are powerful for testing but can feel loose; interviewers check that you define small interfaces where you use them.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A Go interview tests four Go-specific pillars: concurrency (goroutines/channels/select/sync), implicit interfaces, error-as-values, and the stdlib (net/http, context).
Goroutines are lightweight threads; channels synchronize them — prefer channel-based communication over shared-memory locks where practical.
Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly (structural typing) — no 'implements' keyword — which changes how you design for testability.
Errors are values, not exceptions — check them, wrap them with fmt.Errorf and %w, and inspect with errors.Is/As.
context.Context propagates cancellation, timeouts, and request-scoped values — interviewers probe whether you thread it through every blocking call.
Beyond Go idioms, the interview tests general backend depth: system design, database/sql, table-driven testing, and production (observability, graceful shutdown).

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: A Go backend interview evaluates your understanding of Go's distinctive features — goroutines and channels, the interface system, error handling, and the standard library — at the level the role demands. It exists because Go is opinionated and different from Java or Python: its concurrency model, its no-exceptions error handling, and its interfaces-satisfied-by-structure shape how production code is written, and an interviewer must verify you've internalized those idioms. The four Go-specific pillars I anchor on are concurrency, where goroutines are lightweight threads and channels synchronize them and I prefer channel communication over shared-memory locks where practical; interfaces, which are satisfied implicitly with no implements keyword, which changes how I design for testability; error handling, where errors are values I return and check and wrap with fmt.Errorf and %w rather than exceptions; and the standard library, where net/http, context, and io are central. The thing interviewers probe hard is context — whether I thread context.Context through every blocking call so cancellation and timeouts propagate. Beyond the Go idioms, the interview still tests general backend depth: system design, database slash sql, table-driven testing, and production concerns like observability and graceful shutdown. The honest tension is that Go deliberately omits features in favor of a small composable language, so the interview is really testing whether I work with Go's grain rather than fight it.

questions.title: Goroutines and Channels
questions.question: How do goroutines and channels work in Go, and how do they differ from threads in other languages?

sections.content: Go interviews almost always include this. They want to hear that you understand goroutines are lightweight (not OS threads), that channels are the preferred communication mechanism over shared memory, and that you follow Go's motto: 'Do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.'

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Goroutines cost ~2KB of stack** — launch millions of them; OS threads cost ~1MB each and top out at thousands
- **Channels synchronize without locks** — unbuffered channels block sender until receiver is ready, providing built-in coordination
- **`select` multiplexes channels** — listen on multiple channels simultaneously; combine with `context.Done()` for timeout and cancellation
- **Always close channels from the sender** — closing from the receiver causes a panic on the next send; range-over-channel stops on close
- **Goroutine leaks are real bugs** — every goroutine must have an exit path via context cancellation, channel close, or explicit signal

Goroutines are Go's unit of concurrent execution — lightweight, managed by the Go runtime, not the OS. Starting a goroutine costs about 2KB of stack space (vs ~1MB for an OS thread). The runtime's M:N scheduler multiplexes thousands of goroutines onto a small number of OS threads.

Channels are typed conduits for communicating between goroutines. A send blocks until a receiver is ready (for unbuffered channels); a receive blocks until data is available. This synchronization mechanism eliminates the need for explicit locks in most cases.

The key difference from Java threads: goroutines use cooperative scheduling managed by the Go runtime, not preemptive OS scheduling. Channel communication is the idiomatic way to synchronize — if you find yourself reaching for `sync.Mutex`, ask whether a channel pattern would be clearer.

- **Goroutines are cheap** — millions can run concurrently; threads cannot
- **Buffered channels don't block until full** — `make(chan T, n)` holds n items without a receiver
- **`close(ch)` signals no more values** — receivers get zero value + false after close
- **Never close a channel from the receiver** — always close from the sender (the one writing)
- **Goroutine leaks** are real bugs — always provide a way to stop goroutines (context cancellation, close channel)
Write a function `fetchAll(urls []string) []Result` that fetches all URLs concurrently but limits concurrency to 5 at a time using a semaphore pattern with channels.

questions.question: What is a goroutine leak and how do you detect one?
questions.quickAnswer: A goroutine that never exits — waits forever on a channel or timer. Use runtime.NumGoroutine() in tests or pprof's /debug/pprof/goroutine endpoint in production.

questions.question: What is the difference between sync.Mutex and sync.RWMutex?
questions.quickAnswer: RWMutex allows multiple concurrent readers OR one writer. Use when reads vastly outnumber writes — significantly better throughput than Mutex for read-heavy workloads.

questions.title: Go Context — Cancellation and Timeouts
questions.question: What is the `context.Context` package used for in Go, and how do you implement proper cancellation and timeouts?

sections.content: Context is idiomatic Go. They want to see you pass context as the first parameter, use it for cancellation propagation across goroutines, and set deadlines for external calls. Not passing context through the call chain is a red flag in Go code review.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Context is the first parameter** — `func Foo(ctx context.Context, ...)` is idiomatic Go; omitting it is a code review red flag
- **Always `defer cancel()`** — even `WithTimeout` returns a cancel function; deferring prevents timer and goroutine resource leaks
- **Cancellation propagates down the chain** — cancelling a parent context automatically cancels all derived child contexts
- **`context.Canceled` vs `context.DeadlineExceeded`** — check `ctx.Err()` after blocking operations to distinguish manual cancellation from timeout
- **`WithValue` for infrastructure only** — trace IDs and request IDs belong in context; function arguments and business data do not

Context carries request-scoped data, cancellation signals, and deadlines across API boundaries and goroutine boundaries. Every long-running or I/O operation should accept a `context.Context` as its first parameter.

The three context operations you use daily: `context.WithCancel` — manual cancellation (user disconnects, stop button). `context.WithTimeout` — deadline in duration (this DB query must finish in 5 seconds). `context.WithDeadline` — deadline at an absolute time. Each returns a new derived context and a cancel function — always `defer cancel()` to free resources.

Context propagates cancellation down the chain. If the HTTP request's context is cancelled (client disconnected), every downstream call using that context — DB queries, HTTP calls to other services — automatically receives the cancellation signal.

- **Context is the first parameter** — `func Foo(ctx context.Context, ...)` — always
- **Always `defer cancel()`** — even `WithTimeout` returns a cancel; defer prevents timer resource leaks
- **Check `ctx.Err()` after blocking ops** — distinguish cancelled vs timeout
- **Don't store context in structs** — pass explicitly; stored context can't be cancelled by the caller
- **`context.WithValue` for infra concerns only** — trace IDs, request IDs; never for business logic data
